"title": "Learning design rules for selective oxidation catalysts from high-throughput experimentation and artificial intelligence",
"authors": "Lucas Foppa, Christopher Sutton, Luca M Ghiringhelli, Sandip De, Patricia Löser, Stephan A Schunk, Ansgar Schäfer, Matthias Scheffler",

"type_of_paper": "Research article (data-driven catalyst design)",
"executive_summary": "Heterogeneous catalyst design is difficult because the number of good catalysts is very small relative to the practically infinite number of possible materials, and because the full catalytic progression cannot be explicitly modelled by first-principles methods. The authors address this gap by applying the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach to a hybrid experimental-plus-theoretical data set for the selective oxidation of propylene on SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten and phosphorus. Using high-throughput experimentation (HTE), 120 three-component catalyst compositions were synthesized and tested across temperatures between 200 and 400 ºC. The reactivity measured by HTE (yield of oxygenates) was used as the target, while temperature and ten composition-dependent physicochemical parameters derived from density-functional-theory (DFT) free-atom properties were offered as candidate descriptive parameters. The SGD analysis identified temperature, phosphorus content and composition-weighted electronegativity as the key parameters describing high yields towards the value-added oxygenates acrolein and acrylic acid. The resulting SG rules not only reflect the underlying processes associated with high performance but also guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements. Applying the rules, the authors designed four- and five-component catalysts, including a five-component material (ruthenium, tungsten, phosphorus, tellurium and tantalum) achieving an oxygenate yield of 59.60% at 400 ºC, which is more than twice as large as any observation in the training data set. These results demonstrate the potential of the SGD-HTE-&-theory approach to identify generalizable, interpretable rules describing exceptional catalytic performance and to hint at materials significantly more performant than those used in training.",

summary.title: Learning design rules for selective oxidation catalysts from high-throughput experimentation and artificial intelligence
summary.authors: Lucas Foppa, Christopher Sutton, Luca M Ghiringhelli, Sandip De, Patricia Löser, Stephan A Schunk, Ansgar Schäfer, Matthias Scheffler
summary.executive_summary: Heterogeneous catalyst design is difficult because the number of good catalysts is very small relative to the practically infinite number of possible materials, and because the full catalytic progression cannot be explicitly modelled by first-principles methods. The authors address this gap by applying the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach to a hybrid experimental-plus-theoretical data set for the selective oxidation of propylene on SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten and phosphorus. Using high-throughput experimentation (HTE), 120 three-component catalyst compositions were synthesized and tested across temperatures between 200 and 400 ºC. The reactivity measured by HTE (yield of oxygenates) was used as the target, while temperature and ten composition-dependent physicochemical parameters derived from density-functional-theory (DFT) free-atom properties were offered as candidate descriptive parameters. The SGD analysis identified temperature, phosphorus content and composition-weighted electronegativity as the key parameters describing high yields towards the value-added oxygenates acrolein and acrylic acid. The resulting SG rules not only reflect the underlying processes associated with high performance but also guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements. Applying the rules, the authors designed four- and five-component catalysts, including a five-component material (ruthenium, tungsten, phosphorus, tellurium and tantalum) achieving an oxygenate yield of 59.60% at 400 ºC, which is more than twice as large as any observation in the training data set. These results demonstrate the potential of the SGD-HTE-&-theory approach to identify generalizable, interpretable rules describing exceptional catalytic performance and to hint at materials significantly more performant than those used in training.

claims.description: The SGD approach can identify interpretable, chemically meaningful rules associated with exceptional catalytic performance.
The SG rules can guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Heterogeneous catalyst design is difficult because the number of good catalysts is very small relative to the practically infinite number of possible materials, and because the full catalytic progression cannot be explicitly modelled by first-principles methods. The authors address this gap by applying the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach to a hybrid experimental-plus-theoretical data set for the selective oxidation of propylene on SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten and phosphorus. Using high-throughput experimentation (HTE), 120 three-component catalyst compositions were synthesized and tested across temperatures between 200 and 400 ºC. The reactivity measured by HTE (yield of oxygenates) was used as the target, while temperature and ten composition-dependent physicochemical parameters derived from density-functional-theory (DFT) free-atom properties were offered as candidate descriptive parameters. The SGD analysis identified temperature, phosphorus content and composition-weighted electronegativity as the key parameters describing high yields towards the value-added oxygenates acrolein and acrylic acid. The resulting SG rules not only reflect the underlying processes associated with high performance but also guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements. Applying the rules, the authors designed four- and five-component catalysts, including a five-component material (ruthenium, tungsten, phosphorus, tellurium and tantalum) achieving an oxygenate yield of 59.60% at 400 ºC, which is more than twice as large as any observation in the training data set. These results demonstrate the potential of the SGD-HTE-&-theory approach to identify generalizable, interpretable rules describing exceptional catalytic performance and to hint at materials significantly more performant than those used in training.

Research Context
Heterogeneous catalysis involves complex surface reaction networks and dynamic restructuring. First-principles modelling of the full catalytic progression is impractical. High-throughput experimentation tests many materials but cannot decide the next promising ones. Good catalysts are rare relative to the practically infinite number of possible materials. Detailed characterization of each tested material is typically not feasible. Catalytic mechanisms vary with materials and conditions, causing unbalanced performance distributions. Global models minimize average prediction error and may miss the most interesting materials.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study asks how to identify key physicochemical parameters and constraints associated with high performance. The central hypothesis is that the SGD local approach can identify rules associated with high performance. The authors predict that temperature, phosphorus content and electronegativity are key parameters. The authors predict that the SG rules can guide the design of more complex catalysts. The authors predict that the SG rules can hint at materials more performant than those in training.

Methodological Details
The study investigated selective partial oxidation of light alkanes to value-added products. The reaction system studied propylene selective oxidation on SiO2-supported catalysts. The catalysts were three-component compositions containing ruthenium, tungsten and phosphorus. The catalysts were prepared on a SiO2 pseudo-liquid support. Several reaction temperatures between 200 and 400 ºC were examined at each composition. Reactions were carried out in tubular, fixed-bed reactors. The reaction feed included Ar, H2O, N2, O2 and propylene at specified molar rates. The same mass of catalyst was used so that contact time was kept fixed. The target was the yield of oxygenates, defined as acrolein plus acrylic acid over propylene fed. Eleven descriptive parameters were used in the SGD analysis. The candidate parameters were derived from DFT-PBEsol and FHI-aims calculations. The per-element free-atom properties were converted into system-specific properties by composition-weighted averaging. The oxygen content was not included because it is not known from the formulation. The target distribution was highly skewed, with most observations being low performance. The average oxygenates yield over the whole data set was 4.83%. Only 41 measurements out of 1220 had oxygenate yields above 20%. The maximum oxygenates yield value was 26.85%. The selected SG contained only 15 data points, approximately 1.2% of the data set. The average yield of oxygenates in the selected SG was 24.15%.

Procedures And Architectures
The SGD approach starts with the generation of a pool of propositions. For continuous parameters, the propositions are inequalities constraining their values. SGD identifies selectors formed by propositions connected with the AND connector. The selectors select subgroups with the most outstanding distributions of the target values. The approach maximizes a quality function measuring how outstanding specific subselections are. The quality function includes a coverage term controlling the subgroup size. The quality function includes the cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence. The divergence favors subgroups with unusual target values compared to the majority. The divergence favors distributions contained in narrower value ranges. The key parameters were temperature, phosphorus content and composition-weighted electronegativity. The temperature rule highlighted intermediate temperatures within the tested range. The phosphorus rule showed that a relatively high phosphorus content is needed. The electronegativity rule limited the range of Ru contents. Ru is needed for propylene conversion but too much leads to combustion products. The rules were validated with a cross-validation study using 90% of the data. The rules were validated by excluding data points with oxygenate yields lower than 3%. Four-component materials were designed by fixing phosphorus content to 0.60 and Ru content to 0.05. The VÇ elements considered were niobium, tantalum, chromium, molybdenum, tin, antimony and tellurium. The VÇ elements had atomic radii of 1.40 to 1.45 Å. The atomic radius of tungsten is 1.45 Å. The VÇ elements were constrained to have a maximum atomic radius difference of 0.10 Å. The five-component materials fixed VÇ as tellurium and evaluated V^ as molybdenum, niobium, tantalum and antimony. The four-and five-component HTE data contained 746 data points. The selected SG for the four-and five-component data had a cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence of 0.355. The selected SG contained 18 data points, approximately 2.4% of the data set. The rules for the four-and five-component data constrained temperature, electron affinity and electron affinity. The electronegativity and electron affinity are related by VY = V^ + V^.

Key Results
The selected SG had the highest cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence of 0.693. The selected SG contained only 15 data points, approximately 1.2% of the data set. The average yield of oxygenates in the selected SG was 24.15%. The average yield in the SG was five times higher than the average on the whole data set. The SG was described by rules on three descriptive parameters. The temperature rule constrained the temperature to 280 to 300 ºC. The phosphorus rule required a phosphorus content higher than 0.55. The electronegativity rule constrained the value to 3.910 to 4.002 eV. The ranges of variation of the minimum and maximum thresholds were 3.882 to 3.910 eV and 3.989 to 4.031. The SG rules were not strongly affected by variations on the data used for their derivation. The highest yield of oxygenates achieved for each four-component composition is shown by the colors. The catalyst achieving the highest yield of oxygenates was 60.19% at 400 ºC. The highest-yield catalyst contained 0.35 molar fraction of tellurium as VÇ element. The VY value for the highest-yield five-component catalyst was 3.947 eV. The five-component catalyst achieved an oxygenate yield of 59.60% at 400 ºC. The five-component catalyst contained tantalum as V^ element. The oxygenate yields for the four-and five-component catalysts were up to twice as large as those obtained with three-component materials. The highest three-component yield was 26.85%. The four-and five-component catalysts achieved the highest yields at higher temperatures than the three-component systems. The SG rule on the reaction temperature derived from the three-component data is not transferable to the four-component ones. The SG rules correctly describe the experimental trend for the four-component materials. The materials based on niobium, chromium, molybdenum, tin, lead and antimony achieve the highest oxygenate yields at relative lower contents. The agreement between the SG rule and the measured oxygenate yield is reasonable despite higher complexity. The identified four-and five-component catalysts are significantly more complex than the training data set. The SG rules hinted at materials significantly more performant than any observation used in training.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The SG rules reflect the specific underlying processes resulting in outstanding performance. The approach identifies a local behavior associated with exceptional performance. The local modelling approach is suitable for the search of exceptional materials. The structures and functions of exceptional materials are hardly modelled explicitly by theory. The composition-weighted electronegativity, phosphorus content and temperature are key parameters. The SG rules rationalize a local reactivity pattern associated with exceptional catalytic performance. The SG rules guide the design of more complex catalysts. The five-component material is captured by the SG rules. The SG rules can identify generalizable rules describing exceptional performance. The SG rules can hint at materials significantly more performant than those used in training.

Contradictions And Limitations
The SG rules might not identify exceptional materials for arbitrary ruthenium content. The SG rules might not identify exceptional materials for VÇ and V^ elements with significantly different radii. Different mechanisms may operate on these materials which could also lead to exceptional performance. The SGD analysis might need to be performed including new data points covering unexplored portions of the materials space. Similar SG rules are obtained when the data points presenting yield of oxygenates lower than 3% are excluded from training.
